title: Ziusudra/Utnapishtim's ark lands in the Ararat region
place_text: Shuruppak, Iraq to Mount Ararat, Armenia/Turkey

tellings.quote: Landing in the Mount Ararat region okay of uh Armenia turkey area
O man of Shurippak, son of Ubara-Tutu.
The ship took its course to the land of Nisir.
The mountain of Nisir held the ship, it let it not move.

plain: The flood hero of ancient Mesopotamia, known as Ziusudra and as Utnapishtim, brought his ark to rest in the Mount Ararat region of Armenia and Turkey, the researcher Matt LaCroix tells Michels. He points to the old Babylonian flood poem Atrahasis and to the Epic of Gilgamesh, and if he is right, the Mesopotamian flood and the Bible's would be one remembered event. In E. A. Wallis Budge's 1920 British Museum translation of the epic's Eleventh Tablet, Uta-Napishtim tells Gilgamesh the story himself; he is the "man of Shurippak, son of Ubara-Tutu," and he says "The ship took its course to the land of Nisir" and "The mountain of Nisir held the ship, it let it not move." The tablet names its own mountain, Nisir, while Genesis has the ark rest "upon the mountains of Ararat," so putting the landing at Ararat follows Genesis rather than the tablet. Read for what happens, the two stories share a shape: a man warned of a flood, a great boat, a mountain that holds it fast. A story can travel and change its place names while keeping a memory, so the different mountain neither proves nor disproves a link. Ziusudra is the name an older Sumerian telling gives its flood hero, and treating him as the same man as Uta-Napishtim is an identification the tablet alone cannot make.

discussion.by: The Epic of Gilgamish, Tablet XI (translated by E. A. Wallis Budge in The Babylonian Story of the Deluge)
discussion.text: The epic gives Uta-Napishtim as the "man of Shurippak" and says "The mountain of Nisir held the ship", a mountain of its own name, where Genesis has the ark rest "upon the mountains of Ararat" (Genesis 8:4); placing the landing in the Ararat region follows Genesis, not the tablet. Ziusudra is the name the older Sumerian telling gives its flood hero, and joining that name to Uta-Napishtim's is an identification the tablet alone cannot make. The words are from E. A. Wallis Budge's translation (The Babylonian Story of the Deluge, 1920) of the Eleventh Tablet of the Assyrian version, in which Uta-Napishtim tells Gilgamish of the flood.
